transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-21
Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jenna Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Liu (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (CTO, PondRock), Ben Morales (Lead ML Eng), Kai Ito (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
PondRock is evaluating Redwood for a small two-week onramp pilot to validate time-to-first-token and unit economics. Primary concerns: data residency, KMS, SSO, and predictable latency at 50-200 qps. Redwood to provide credits and quickstart artifacts; agree to run bench next week.

Action items (captured from meeting): see metadata.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jenna Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um I'm Jenna, AE on the Redwood side, and we got Marcus from SE. How's everybody doing?
[00:07] Aisha Khan: Good thanks. Sorry joining from the west coast, slight delay.
[00:12] Marcus Liu: Morning! Thanks for carving time. Quick goal for today: understand your constraints and see if the two-week pilot with credits makes sense.
[00:22] Kai Ito: Hi, yeah we want to validate "time to first token" in our stack and also understand what it would look like if we go private or stay hosted.
[00:31] Ben Morales: Specifically latency at 50 qps and cost per 1k tokens -- and also if we can keep everything within our EU region for data residency.
[00:40] Jenna Park: Great — that's exactly what others do with the PLG onramp. We typically spin up a trial project, push some credits, and provide a quickstart notebook. Marcus will talk about the steps technically.
[00:52] Marcus Liu: Yeah so on the tech side you can do a curl first call in like two minutes. There's a small SDK and a docker sample if you want to simulate requests. For a TTFT test I usually recommend a short script that nukes the cold start, so you get realistic numbers.
[01:09] Ben Morales: When you say "curl in two minutes" do you mean for hosted Redwood API? Or does that differ for Dedicated/Private?
[01:16] Marcus Liu: For hosted it's that quick. Dedicated or Private — there's extra setup: VPC, network peering, maybe a data plane connector, so it's more like a few hours to a day depending on your infra.
[01:27] Aisha Khan: Our security team will likely push for VPC or private deployment, but the timeline is tight. Would the hosted credits be enough for a first bench?
[01:36] Jenna Park: Clients often start hosted to get TTFT and UX validation, then move to a Dedicated or Private pilot for longer-term compliance. Hosted can be scoped to EU region and we have SOC 2 and audit logs. We'll attach the security pack.
[01:48] Kai Ito: You mentioned audit logs — do we get request-level logs for regulatory reasons?
[01:52] Marcus Liu: Yes, request-level logs are available and can be sent to your log destination. For Private we can integrate with your KMS/HSM for key control. For Hosted we support customer-managed keys via KMS in some tiers.
[02:06] Ben Morales: Any limitations on streaming or function calls in the trial?
[02:10] Jenna Park: No, the trial supports streaming and function/tool calling; the only limits are quota-based which we can raise for pilot.
[02:18] [Background interruption — door closing]
[02:21] Aisha Khan: Quick question on cost baseline — do you have sample cost per 1k token numbers for the small models? We want to compare with our in-house quantized model.
[02:29] Marcus Liu: We'll send a model cost matrix, but a rough ballpark: small open models on hosted at our default quantization profile are X units per 1k tokens — I'll put exact numbers in the follow-up. Note that batching and KV cache can lower effective cost for repeated prompts.
[02:46] Ben Morales: How does Redis prefix caching or KV cache work with Redwood? Does it require changes in the model?
[02:52] Marcus Liu: No model changes. Prefix/KV caching is at the request routing layer — for chat-like flows we keep the KV cache warm and that reduces per-token compute. It's automatic if you enable it in the route settings.
[03:07] Kai Ito: For the TTFT run we want to replicate our front-end pattern: short prompts, then a longer follow-up where the KV gets used. Is that possible in the notebook?
[03:14] Marcus Liu: Yep, we'll include a sample that simulates that flow.
[03:19] Jenna Park: For the two-week pilot idea: we give X dollars of credits, you run a few bench patterns, and we'll help observe latency and token spend. If the pilot looks good you can either continue on hosted credits, reserve Dedicated, or evaluate Private.
[03:34] Aisha Khan: Can you call that out in the email: what is included, what we have to provision, and what Redwood does? Our procurement team needs that.
[03:42] Jenna Park: Absolutely. We'll send a one-pager pilot scope: included items, roles, expected timelines.
[03:48] Ben Morales: On network side, if we start hosted but later move to VPC, do you support seamless model pinning and rollouts? We don't want to rewrite client code.
[03:58] Marcus Liu: Yes — the API surface is consistent. You can pin model versions and rollout policies in the console, and the SDKs use the same endpoints. Moving to VPC just changes the network/display rules not the client code.
[04:11] Kai Ito: What's the onboarding path for single sign on? We use Okta and SCIM.
[04:16] Jenna Park: We support SSO via SAML/Okta and SCIM for provisioning. We'll attach the SSO guide and a configuration checklist.
[04:25] [00:04:30 timestamp drift — transcript auto-stamp]
[04:29] Aisha Khan: One thing: our compliance folks will ask about data retention. If we use hosted do logs persist? Are they deletable?
[04:37] Marcus Liu: You control retention windows; we can configure auto-delete or export to your storage. For Private, logs stay in your environment. For hosted, we have configurable retention policies and you can request immediate deletion under certain contracts.
[04:52] Ben Morales: For the bench, we want to run a 20-minute spike test to 200 qps to see throttling -- is that something you'd run with us?
[04:59] Jenna Park: We can coordinate a bench session. Marcus, will you run the bench?
[05:03] Marcus Liu: Yes, happy to run it with your team. We'll do a short run first to warm caches, then the full spike. We'll capture p95/p99 and token bill.
[05:12] Kai Ito: If the p99 is high during spike, do you have fallback policies or model variants that can be used automatically?
[05:19] Marcus Liu: Yes — we support routing policies and automatic fallbacks to cheaper model variants or different regions. That said, for strict latency apps you should talk about Dedicated with reserved capacity.
[05:30] Aisha Khan: What's the expected realistic TTFT for our stack? We run nodejs backend with an express endpoint and use a small caching layer.
[05:38] Marcus Liu: For a simple curl via hosted, customers report median cold-start TTFTs of 300-600ms depending on model and length. If you pre-warm or keep a small idle pool, it's lower. For our runtime, the initial handshake, tokenization, and first chunk streaming are the main costs. We'll help you tune that.
[05:56] Ben Morales: Do you have example benchmarks on the console we can look at?
[05:59] Jenna Park: Yes, model perf pages in the catalog show latency profiles. We'll point you to the EU region pages.
[06:07] [06:07 — short crosstalk]
[06:10] Aisha Khan: About legal paperwork — NDA already signed but procurement will need terms for pilot, is there a template?
[06:16] Jenna Park: We have a pilot order form and standard terms. For enterprise pilots we can add simple MSA addendum for data specifics. I'll cc the legal contact.
[06:24] Ben Morales: On instrumentation, do we get token-level cost breakdowns? We want per-route and per-caller metrics.
[06:31] Marcus Liu: Yes the console has per-route token breakdowns and you can attach tracing hooks. The billing export gives per-token granularity.
[06:38] Kai Ito: For the quickstart, what's a realistic minimal integration checklist?
[06:43] Marcus Liu: Minimal checklist: 1) create trial project and API key, 2) run sample curl/SDK, 3) run the TTFT notebook, 4) run a small traffic sim, 5) review logs and cost. We include sample scripts.
[06:58] Aisha Khan: One logistical question: we have an internal policy that all keys should rotate every 30 days. Are your API keys compatible with rotation and programmatic creation?
[07:07] Marcus Liu: Yes keys can be rotated and you can generate scoped tokens. We also support short-lived tokens for internal tooling.
[07:13] Ben Morales: Does the trial include function/tool calling? We use some tool integrations to fetch structured data for prompts.
[07:19] Jenna Park: Trial includes tooling and streaming, no disabled features. Some advanced enterprise integrations might be gated but function calling is available in trial.
[07:28] Kai Ito: For the pilot success criteria — what do you recommend?
[07:33] Jenna Park: Typical criteria: TTFT less than X ms median, p95 under Y ms for 95% of requests, predictable cost below Z per 1k tokens, and security checklist items signed off. We'll help set thresholds.
[07:47] Aisha Khan: Can you send a sample threshold template? That would help prod and infra agree.
[07:52] Jenna Park: Yes we'll add a success criteria template in the follow-up.
[07:57] [07:57 — brief pause]
[08:00] Ben Morales: About the free credits — is there a mechanism to allocate to specific teams and track per-team usage?
[08:06] Jenna Park: The console supports projects/orgs and you can split credits. We'll show how to create sub-projects and set budgets.
[08:13] Kai Ito: If we later bring this on-prem, is there an on-prem package? How different is it from private VPC?
[08:20] Marcus Liu: We have a Private on-prem package and a VPC-hosted private option. On-prem requires more ops work — install packages, connectivity for control plane can be optional, and you get local KMS. VPC is often a middle ground.
[08:34] Aisha Khan: Any customers who started hosted and moved to private for compliance? Names are fine to share.
[08:39] Jenna Park: Yes — we can share anonymized case studies. I'll include a short list.
[08:44] Ben Morales: Ok last technical: do you have a recommended quantization profile for minimizing latency in our use case? We run short response chat mostly.
[08:52] Marcus Liu: For chat with short responses we recommend 4-bit quantization profile Q4x if your tolerances are okay; it often hits a good latency/cost point. We'll propose a model and quantization in the tech follow-up.
[09:05] Kai Ito: Great. Sounds like we have a plan.
[09:08] Jenna Park: Next steps recap: Marcus will send quickstart repo and TTFT notebook; I'll push trial credits and send pilot scope + security pack; Ben will send sample payloads and Aisha will confirm pilot stakeholders.
[09:21] Aisha Khan: Works for us. Can we target the bench next Tuesday?
[09:25] Marcus Liu: Yes I'm available Tuesday 2026-12-28 UTC morning — I'll propose times in the calendar invite.
[09:32] Jenna Park: I'll send calendar invites and the follow-up email after the call. Thanks everyone.
[09:37] [End of recording — closing pleasantries and dropouts]
